questions.q: After calculating a 12% increase in quantity supplied from an 8% price increase, a student reports PES = 0.67. Which step is wrong?
options: The ratio was inverted; PES = 12%/8% = 1.5
The supply response should be given a negative sign
The percentage changes should be added to get 20
The calculation should use the original price level instead
questions.feedback: Price elasticity of supply divides the percentage change in quantity supplied by the percentage change in price, so 12%/8% = 1.5.

questions.q: A learner says unused production capacity makes supply less elastic. What is the correction?
options: Unused capacity fixes quantity supplied at one level
Unused capacity affects demand elasticity but not supply
Unused capacity guarantees perfectly elastic supply
Unused capacity usually makes it easier to expand output, increasing supply elasticity
questions.feedback: Spare capacity lets firms respond to higher prices without first building entirely new capacity.

questions.q: A learner says input mobility has no effect on supply elasticity. Best repair?
options: Only demand-side substitutes affect elasticity
Input mobility changes the sign of supply elasticity
Inputs that can be reallocated easily generally make supply more elastic
Input mobility makes supply perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: Flexible inputs let producers change output more readily when price changes.

questions.q: A learner gets PES = 0.4 and calls supply elastic. What should be corrected?
options: The sign alone determines elastic versus inelastic
A coefficient below one is inelastic over the measured range
Any positive coefficient is elastic
A coefficient below one is perfectly elastic
questions.feedback: For PES, magnitude below one means quantity supplied responds proportionally less than price.

questions.q: A commodity price rises 10% and quantity supplied rises 15%. Which adjacent production conclusion fits the elasticity result?
options: Producers show an elastic supply response
Producers show an inelastic supply response
Quantity supplied did not respond
The result measures demand, not supply
questions.feedback: A 15% quantity response to a 10% price change gives PES above one.

questions.q: Why does a longer time horizon often connect supply elasticity to investment decisions?
options: Longer horizons make all prices fixed
Firms lose the ability to change inputs over time
Supply becomes unrelated to marginal cost
Firms have more time to add capacity and reorganize production
questions.feedback: Investment and capacity adjustment make long-run supply more responsive.

questions.q: How does inventory management connect to supply elasticity?
options: Inventory affects only consumer demand
Stored goods make supply vertical by definition
Stored inventory can be released when price rises, increasing quantity responsiveness
Inventory prevents firms from reacting to price
questions.feedback: Storage creates another margin through which sellers can respond to price changes.

questions.q: A market has highly mobile labor and equipment. What does that suggest about the supply response to a price increase?
options: The price increase cannot affect production
Output can adjust more strongly because inputs can move toward the market
Output must remain fixed because mobile inputs leave the market
Demand becomes more elastic while supply is unchanged
questions.feedback: Input mobility links production flexibility to greater supply elasticity.

questions.q: A learner sees income elasticity of -0.5 and labels the good a necessity. What is the repair?
options: The negative sign identifies an inferior good for the measured consumers
Any coefficient below one identifies a normal necessity
Negative income elasticity means the goods are complements
The coefficient measures price responsiveness, not income responsiveness
questions.feedback: Negative income elasticity means demand falls when income rises.

questions.q: Income rises 10% and quantity demanded rises 5%. A learner reports income elasticity of 2. What went wrong?
options: The sign should be negative because income rose
The correct value is 15 because percentages are added
Income elasticity cannot be calculated from percentage changes
The ratio was reversed; the elasticity is 0.5
questions.feedback: Income elasticity is %ΔQd divided by %Δincome, so 5%/10% = 0.5.

questions.q: A grocery chain expects household incomes to rise. Which use of income elasticity is most direct?
options: Calculate the money multiplier
Find the slope of the supply curve
Forecast which product categories may gain or lose demand
Determine the legal incidence of a sales tax
questions.feedback: Income elasticity helps firms anticipate demand shifts as consumer income changes.

questions.q: A category has income elasticity 1.4. How does that connect to business forecasting during an expansion?
options: The category must be a complement to every other good
Demand may grow more than proportionally with income
Demand must fall as income rises
Quantity supplied must fall by 1.4%
questions.feedback: An elasticity above one indicates a strong positive demand response to income growth.

questions.q: Why can income elasticity help explain changes in the mix of goods consumers buy as an economy grows?
options: Normal, luxury, and inferior goods respond differently to rising income
All goods have identical income responses
Income elasticity measures only producer costs
It fixes consumer preferences at one bundle
questions.feedback: Different income responses shift the composition of demand as purchasing power changes.

questions.q: A learner sees cross-price elasticity of +0.9 and says the goods are complements. What is the repair?
options: A positive coefficient indicates complements
The sign identifies normal versus inferior goods
Cross-price elasticity cannot classify related goods
A positive coefficient indicates substitutes
questions.feedback: Demand for one good moves with the other good’s price when the goods are substitutes.

questions.q: The price of good Y rises 8% and demand for good X rises 4%. A learner reports cross-price elasticity of 2. What is the repair?
options: The ratio is 12 because the percentages are added
Cross-price elasticity uses X’s own price change
The ratio is 4%/8% = 0.5
The ratio must be negative because price rose
questions.feedback: Cross-price elasticity divides the percentage change in demand for X by the percentage change in the price of Y.

questions.q: A coffee shop tracks the price of a nearby competitor’s drinks. Why is cross-price elasticity useful?
options: It determines the legal tax rate
It indicates how the competitor’s price may shift demand for the shop’s drinks
It measures the shop’s fixed cost
It identifies the money supply
questions.feedback: Cross-price elasticity connects substitute pricing to demand shifts.

questions.q: A console maker lowers console prices. Why might a game publisher care about cross-price elasticity?
options: Negative cross-price elasticity would imply game demand rises as console price falls
Positive income elasticity guarantees game demand falls
Supply elasticity determines whether consoles and games are complements
Cross-price elasticity is unrelated to complementary products
questions.feedback: Complementary goods connect through opposite movements between one price and the other good’s demand.

questions.q: Two brands have cross-price elasticity near +2. What strategic connection does that suggest?
options: They are strong complements
They are unrelated goods
They must have identical marginal costs
Their demand is strongly linked as substitutes
questions.feedback: A large positive cross-price coefficient signals a strong substitution relationship.

questions.q: A learner calculates total revenue by adding price and quantity. What is the repair?
options: Divide price by quantity
Add consumer and producer surplus
Multiply price by quantity sold
Subtract quantity from price
questions.feedback: Total revenue is P × Q.

questions.q: A learner says a price cut always lowers total revenue because each unit sells for less. What is missing?
options: A price cut always makes demand inelastic
Quantity may rise enough to increase revenue when demand is elastic
Quantity demanded never changes with price
Revenue depends only on fixed cost
questions.feedback: The total-revenue test compares the price change with the percentage quantity response.

questions.q: A learner says marginal revenue must be positive everywhere on a downward-sloping demand curve. What is the repair?
options: Marginal revenue becomes zero near unit elasticity and negative on the inelastic portion
Marginal revenue is always equal to price
Marginal revenue is negative only when demand is perfectly elastic
Elasticity has no relationship to marginal revenue
questions.feedback: For a standard downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion, zero near unit elasticity, and negative on the inelastic portion.

questions.q: How does the total-revenue formula connect a demand curve to firm revenue?
options: The demand slope directly equals total revenue
Revenue is the area above demand and below price
Quantity alone determines revenue
Each price-quantity point implies revenue equal to P × Q
questions.feedback: A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue.

questions.q: A firm cuts price and revenue rises. What demand-side conclusion can management carry into pricing decisions?
options: Quantity demanded must have fallen
Price and quantity effects always cancel
Customers were responsive enough for the quantity gain to dominate
Demand was perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: The total-revenue test translates elasticity into a practical pricing signal.

questions.q: Why is unit elasticity a useful benchmark for revenue management on a linear demand curve?
options: It makes demand perfectly horizontal
It is near the point where total revenue is maximized
It guarantees profit is maximized regardless of cost
It makes marginal cost zero
questions.feedback: At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.

questions.q: How does elasticity connect to marginal-revenue reasoning for a firm with downward-sloping demand?
options: MR is positive on the elastic portion and negative on the inelastic portion
MR is always zero when price changes
Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than MR
MR is positive only when demand is perfectly inelastic
questions.feedback: The elasticity region helps identify the sign of marginal revenue.

questions.q: A tax raises the price buyers pay. Why can demand elasticity matter for the seller’s revenue response?
options: It fixes the statutory tax rate
It determines the seller’s fixed cost
It guarantees producer surplus rises
It determines how strongly quantity demanded falls as the buyer price rises
questions.feedback: Revenue consequences depend on the quantity response to the effective price change.

questions.q: A seller receives $18 per unit on 400 units after a market change. What concept links this outcome to elasticity analysis?
options: Producer surplus always equals total revenue
Cross-price elasticity equals $18 × 400
Total revenue equals the price received times quantity sold
Consumer surplus equals price times quantity
questions.feedback: Elasticity analysis often evaluates how price and quantity changes combine to change revenue.

questions.q: A learner says a price-based policy will reduce quantity by the same percentage in every market. What is the repair?
options: Elasticity affects revenue but not policy responses
Quantity response depends on the relevant elasticity
Every market has unit-elastic demand
Only supply shifts can change quantity
questions.feedback: More elastic buyers or sellers respond more strongly to price incentives.

questions.q: A learner says labor demand elasticity is unrelated to substitution possibilities. Best correction?
options: More available substitutes for a type of labor generally make labor demand more elastic
Substitutes make labor demand perfectly inelastic
Factor demand elasticity depends only on worker preferences
Substitution changes labor supply but never labor demand
questions.feedback: Employers can respond more strongly to wage changes when alternative inputs are available.

questions.q: A learner says supply elasticity does not matter when an export price rises. What is the repair?
options: Export prices affect demand only
Supply elasticity matters only in closed markets
More elastic supply means output cannot change
More elastic supply allows a larger output response to the higher price
questions.feedback: Trade price changes generate larger production responses when supply is more elastic.

questions.q: How does a demand curve connect to willingness to pay?
options: Its height represents marginal willingness to pay for successive units
Its slope measures seller fixed cost
Its area below price is producer surplus
It shows willingness to accept
questions.feedback: Demand can be interpreted as buyers’ marginal willingness to pay.

questions.q: Why is consumer surplus drawn below demand and above the market price?
options: The area measures seller cost above price
The area equals tax revenue by definition
The demand curve is a supply schedule
The vertical gap is willingness to pay minus price for units purchased
questions.feedback: Consumer surplus is the buyer value-price gap across purchased units.

questions.q: A price decrease lets an existing buyer pay less for the same unit. What happens to that buyer’s surplus?
options: It becomes producer surplus
It is unchanged because the buyer already purchased
It rises by the amount of the price decrease, holding willingness to pay fixed
It falls because lower prices reduce value
questions.feedback: A lower price widens the gap between willingness to pay and price.

questions.q: How does consumer surplus contribute to total surplus?
options: It is excluded from efficiency analysis
It is the buyer-side component added to producer surplus
It replaces producer surplus in total-surplus calculations
It equals total revenue
questions.feedback: Total surplus combines buyer and seller gains.

questions.q: How does a supply curve connect to willingness to accept?
options: Its height represents the marginal seller’s opportunity cost or minimum acceptable amount
Its height represents buyer willingness to pay
Its area above price is consumer surplus
It fixes market demand
questions.feedback: Supply can be interpreted as the marginal cost or willingness to accept of successive units.

questions.q: Why is producer surplus drawn above supply and below the market price?
options: The area is buyer willingness to pay minus price
The area equals total revenue
Supply above price measures consumer surplus
The vertical gap is price received minus seller cost for units sold
questions.feedback: Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied.

questions.q: A higher market price is paid for the same unit while seller cost is unchanged. What happens to producer surplus on that unit?
options: It becomes consumer surplus
It is unchanged
It rises
It falls
questions.feedback: A higher price widens the price-minus-cost gap received by the seller.

questions.q: A learner treats consumer surplus and producer surplus as competing measures and keeps only the larger one. What is the repair?
options: Only consumer surplus counts toward efficiency
Total surplus adds both buyer and seller surplus
Total surplus always equals the larger side
Producer surplus replaces consumer surplus at equilibrium
questions.feedback: The efficiency measure combines gains on both sides of the market.

questions.q: A learner says any voluntary trade creates gains even when seller cost exceeds buyer value. What is the repair?
options: A trade creates positive total gains only when buyer value is at least seller cost
Voluntary exchange always creates positive measured surplus regardless of values
Seller cost is irrelevant to gains from trade
Buyer value matters only after the trade occurs
questions.feedback: The buyer-seller value gap determines whether the exchange adds surplus.

questions.q: How does total surplus connect consumer and producer surplus in a market-equilibrium graph?
options: It is only the rectangle of total revenue
It excludes producer gains
It counts only trades above equilibrium quantity
It combines the buyer area above price and seller area below price
questions.feedback: Total surplus is the combined area between demand and supply for traded units.

questions.q: How does opportunity cost enter gains-from-exchange analysis?
options: Only buyer income determines whether trade creates gains
Gains exist whenever price is positive
Seller willingness to accept reflects the value of resources given up
Opportunity cost is excluded from producer decisions
questions.feedback: Exchange gains compare buyer value with seller opportunity cost.

questions.q: A policy shifts surplus from buyers to sellers without changing trades. What does total-surplus analysis add?
options: It ignores producer gains
It reveals that the change is distributional rather than an efficiency loss
It proves buyers are better off
It treats every transfer as deadweight loss
questions.feedback: Adding both sides separates transfers from destroyed gains.

questions.q: Why does comparative advantage ultimately matter for gains from exchange?
options: Specialization can create additional mutually beneficial trades and larger total gains
Comparative advantage guarantees equal surplus for everyone
It eliminates opportunity cost
It makes all world prices identical
questions.feedback: Comparative advantage expands the potential gains available from exchange.

questions.q: A learner keeps producing after the next seller’s cost exceeds the next buyer’s value. What is the repair?
options: Keep producing because more output always raises surplus
Ignore seller cost when buyers still want the good
Produce until consumer surplus becomes zero
Stop before units whose marginal cost exceeds marginal willingness to pay
questions.feedback: Units with cost above value reduce total surplus.

questions.q: A learner allocates scarce units to the lowest-value buyers because they “need a bargain.” What does efficiency require?
options: Allocate units to the highest-cost sellers
Efficiency requires equal surplus for every buyer
Allocate units to the highest willingness-to-pay buyers, holding other assumptions fixed
Allocate units randomly regardless of value
questions.feedback: The standard surplus criterion maximizes gains by placing goods with the highest-value users.

questions.q: A learner assigns production to the highest-cost sellers because they need the highest price. What is the efficiency repair?
options: Efficiency requires identical costs across firms
Use lower-cost sellers first
Use higher-cost sellers first
Seller cost does not affect total surplus
questions.feedback: Producing with lower opportunity-cost sellers preserves more surplus.

questions.q: A learner calls the buyer with the highest willingness to pay the marginal buyer. What is the correction?
options: The marginal buyer is the last buyer just willing to purchase at the market price
The marginal buyer is always the richest buyer
The marginal buyer is the first buyer in the market
The marginal buyer is a seller at the equilibrium quantity
questions.feedback: Marginal refers to the edge of participation, not the maximum willingness to pay.

questions.q: A learner says an outcome is efficient whenever consumer surplus is maximized. What is missing?
options: Efficiency ignores sellers entirely
Consumer surplus and total surplus are identical
Efficiency means price must be zero
Efficiency uses total surplus, including producer surplus
questions.feedback: Market efficiency is judged by combined buyer and seller gains.

questions.q: A learner says the efficient quantity is where price is lowest. What is the repair?
options: Efficiency depends only on fixed cost
The efficient quantity is always zero under scarcity
The efficient quantity is where marginal buyer value and marginal seller cost cross
The lowest price always maximizes total surplus
questions.feedback: Efficiency compares marginal willingness to pay with marginal willingness to accept.

questions.q: How does marginal analysis connect to the efficient quantity?
options: Ignore the next unit and compare only totals
Produce additional units while marginal benefit is at least marginal cost
Produce until average cost is minimized regardless of demand
Stop whenever total revenue rises
questions.feedback: The efficient stopping rule is a marginal benefit-versus-marginal cost comparison.

questions.q: How does efficient allocation connect to opportunity cost?
options: Use resources where buyer value exceeds the opportunity cost by the greatest amount
Ignore opportunity cost once a market price exists
Give production to the highest-cost supplier
Allocate goods to minimize consumer surplus
questions.feedback: Surplus measures the value created above the opportunity cost of resources used.

questions.q: Why do the marginal buyer and seller help identify equilibrium efficiency?
options: They determine the money supply
They set every firm’s fixed cost
They identify the highest consumer income
They mark the edge where willingness to pay and willingness to accept determine whether one more trade adds gains
questions.feedback: The last feasible trade reveals the marginal gain from extending quantity.

questions.q: A price control changes the quantity traded away from the competitive quantity. What efficiency question should surplus analysis ask?
options: Did every buyer pay the same tax?
Did nominal GDP change?
Are mutually beneficial trades lost or inefficient trades created?
Did the legal price change labels on the graph?
questions.feedback: Efficiency focuses on how the policy changes the set of value-creating trades.

questions.q: How does the supply-and-demand intersection relate to the surplus criterion in the basic competitive model?
options: It makes all buyers identical
It identifies the quantity where marginal willingness to pay equals marginal willingness to accept
It guarantees equal consumer and producer surplus
It identifies the maximum possible market price
questions.feedback: The intersection matches the marginal value-cost condition for efficient quantity.

questions.q: A learner counts a $20 transfer from consumers to producers as a $20 deadweight loss. What is the repair?
options: A transfer changes who receives surplus; deadweight loss requires gains that disappear
Every transfer is a deadweight loss
Producer gains are excluded from total surplus
Consumer losses never affect welfare
questions.feedback: Efficiency loss comes from destroyed gains, not from a dollar merely moving between groups.

questions.q: A learner says the market outcome with the highest consumer-plus-producer surplus must also be the fairest. What is the repair?
options: Highest total surplus guarantees equal distribution
Fairness is measured only by producer surplus
Equity is identical to willingness to pay
Efficiency and equity are separate criteria
questions.feedback: Total surplus measures efficiency, while fairness requires additional value judgments.

questions.q: How does surplus analysis connect to normative economics?
options: Any efficient market is normatively fair
Equity is determined mechanically by the equilibrium price
Efficiency can be measured with surplus, but equity judgments require values about distribution
Normative economics eliminates the need to measure efficiency
questions.feedback: The efficiency result is positive analysis; deciding whether the distribution is fair adds a normative criterion.

questions.q: Why might an externality require extending ordinary consumer-plus-producer surplus analysis?
options: Externalities matter only for income distribution
Third-party costs or benefits are not fully captured by private surplus
Externalities automatically raise consumer surplus
Producer surplus already includes every social cost
questions.feedback: Social surplus must include effects on people outside the transaction.

questions.q: A learner says the world price is the same thing as the country’s no-trade equilibrium price. What is the repair?
options: The world price is the external trading price; comparing it with the no-trade price reveals importer or exporter status
The two prices must always be equal
The world price is domestic producer surplus
The no-trade price is set by foreign supply only
questions.feedback: Trade status comes from comparing the world price with the domestic autarky equilibrium price.

questions.q: A learner calculates imports as domestic supply minus domestic demand. What is the repair?
options: Imports equal supply plus demand
Imports equal world price minus domestic price
Imports equal domestic production only
Imports equal domestic quantity demanded minus domestic quantity supplied
questions.feedback: In an importing market, excess domestic demand is filled by imports.

questions.q: A learner calculates exports as domestic demand minus domestic supply. What is the repair?
options: Exports equal world price times domestic demand
Exports equal domestic consumption only
Exports equal domestic quantity supplied minus domestic quantity demanded
Exports equal demand plus supply
questions.feedback: In an exporting market, excess domestic supply is sold abroad.

questions.q: A learner says opening an importing market to a lower world price reduces domestic consumption. What is the correction?
options: Only production can change with trade
The lower domestic price generally increases quantity demanded
The lower price decreases quantity demanded
Consumption is fixed after trade opens
questions.feedback: Consumers respond to the lower price by demanding more.

questions.q: A learner says a lower world price in an importing market increases domestic production. What is the repair?
options: The lower domestic price generally reduces quantity supplied by domestic firms
A lower price always raises domestic production
Domestic output is fixed by the world price
Imports cannot affect domestic producers
questions.feedback: Domestic producers move along supply to a lower quantity at the lower price.

questions.q: How does the import quantity connect to ordinary market disequilibrium at the world price?
options: Imports are the same as a domestic shortage under a binding ceiling
Imports equal total domestic production
Imports are unrelated to supply and demand
Imports fill the gap between domestic quantity demanded and domestic quantity supplied
questions.feedback: At the world price, excess domestic demand is met through imports.

questions.q: How does export quantity connect to ordinary supply-and-demand analysis at the world price?
options: Exports occur only when domestic supply shifts left
Exports are determined without reference to price
Exports are the excess of domestic quantity supplied over domestic quantity demanded
Exports equal domestic quantity demanded
questions.feedback: At the world price, excess domestic supply is sold to foreign buyers.

questions.q: A learner says free trade cannot create net gains if one domestic group loses. What is the repair?
options: Distributional losses are never counted
Net gains can be positive when winners gain more than losers lose
Any losing group makes total surplus negative
Trade gains require every person to gain
questions.feedback: Aggregate gains and distribution are separate: a market can have positive net gains and identifiable losers.

questions.q: How does the surplus framework connect free-trade winners and losers to the efficiency conclusion?
options: Add consumer and producer surplus changes to determine the net gain
Count only the group that gains
Ignore producer surplus in importing markets
Treat every redistribution as deadweight loss
questions.feedback: The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison.

questions.q: A learner calculates tariff revenue using all domestic consumption rather than imported units. What is the repair?
options: Multiply the tariff by domestic production plus imports
Use the world price times all consumption
Tariff revenue equals consumer surplus lost
Multiply the tariff per unit by the quantity imported
questions.feedback: The tariff is collected on imported units, not on every unit consumed.

questions.q: A learner says all consumer surplus lost under a tariff is deadweight loss. What is the repair?
options: Producer gains are not part of total surplus
Government revenue is always deadweight loss
Some loss is transferred to producers and government; only the unrecovered portion is deadweight loss
All consumer loss disappears from national welfare
questions.feedback: Tariff welfare analysis separates transfers from production and consumption distortions.

questions.q: How does a tariff connect to the tax-wedge idea from domestic markets?
options: It guarantees the legal and economic burden are identical
It creates a wedge between the world price and the domestic buyer/seller price
It eliminates the role of price
It shifts world demand only
questions.feedback: A tariff acts like a tax on imports and raises the domestic price above the world price in the small-country model.

questions.q: How does tariff deadweight loss connect to surplus analysis?
options: It is the total surplus destroyed by production and consumption distortions
It is the full transfer from consumers to producers
It equals tariff revenue
It is producer surplus after the tariff
questions.feedback: The surplus framework identifies the trades and resource uses that no longer maximize gains.

questions.q: A learner says quota rent is government revenue automatically. What is the repair?
options: Quota rent is always collected as a tariff
Quota rent equals domestic producer surplus
Quota rent exists only when the quota is nonbinding
Quota rent goes to whoever holds the valuable import rights unless the government auctions them
questions.feedback: Unlike tariff revenue, quota rent depends on who receives or buys the import licenses.

questions.q: A learner says equal-price tariffs and quotas must have identical national effects. What key issue is missing?
options: Whether imports exist
Whether domestic firms produce anything
Who receives the quota rents
Whether consumers face a price
questions.feedback: If foreign license holders capture quota rents, national surplus differs from an equivalent tariff with domestic government revenue.

questions.q: How does a binding quota connect to ordinary supply-and-demand pressure?
options: Import restrictions make domestic supply irrelevant
Restricting imports reduces available supply to the domestic market and raises the domestic price
A quota shifts domestic demand left automatically
A quota fixes the world price and domestic price at zero
questions.feedback: The quantity restriction tightens the domestic market and raises price until the permitted import gap is satisfied.

questions.q: How does quota rent connect to economic rent more generally?
options: A scarce legal right can acquire value because it permits profitable access
Quota rent is a payment for labor only
Economic rent requires a perfectly competitive labor market
Quota rent equals consumer surplus by definition
questions.feedback: Import licenses become valuable because the restriction creates a price gap.

questions.q: Why can auctioning quota licenses make a quota look more like a tariff in national-welfare accounting?
options: Auctioning eliminates the domestic price increase
Auctioning makes imports unlimited
Auctioning turns the quota into an export subsidy
The government captures the quota rent much like tariff revenue
questions.feedback: Who receives the rent is a major difference between quotas and tariffs.

questions.q: A demand increase occurs under a fixed quota. What does the quota teach about quantity controls versus price-based barriers?
options: Both price and imports must stay unchanged
The quota automatically becomes a tariff
The import quantity stays capped while domestic price can rise further
Domestic price stays fixed while imports expand freely
questions.feedback: A hard quantity limit adjusts differently from a fixed per-unit tariff when market conditions change.

questions.q: If foreign exporters capture quota rents, what adjacent distributional question should policy analysis ask?
options: Whether the world price becomes the autarky price
Whether part of the domestic consumer loss becomes income to foreigners rather than domestic revenue
Whether domestic demand becomes perfectly elastic
Whether producer surplus is always zero
questions.feedback: Rent ownership affects the national distribution and welfare consequences of a quota.

questions.q: How does a quota-versus-tariff comparison connect to policy design?
options: Two policies can create similar price and quantity effects but differ in who receives the transfer
All trade restrictions have identical distributional effects
Only quotas create deadweight loss
Tariffs never affect domestic producers
questions.feedback: Policy evaluation must track both efficiency distortions and the destination of rents or revenue.

questions.q: How does evaluating protection connect positive and normative economics?
options: Positive economics decides which distribution is fair
Normative economics calculates tariff revenue mechanically
The two approaches are identical in trade policy
Positive analysis estimates costs and benefits; normative judgment weighs goals and distribution
questions.feedback: Trade-policy evaluation separates what a policy does from judgments about whether its goals justify those effects.
